{{short description|Theorem in quantum mechanics}}
In [[quantum mechanics]], '''Kramers' theorem''' or '''Kramers' degeneracy theorem''' states that for every energy [[eigenstate]] of a [[T-symmetry|time-reversal symmetric]] system with half-integer total [[Spin (physics)|spin]], there is another eigenstate with the same energy related by time-reversal. In other words, the [[Degeneracy (quantum mechanics)|degeneracy]] of every energy level is an even number if it has half-integer spin. The theorem is named after Dutch physicist [[Hendrik Anthony Kramers|H. A. Kramers]].

In theoretical physics, the [[T-symmetry|time reversal symmetry]] is the symmetry of physical laws under a time reversal transformation:
:<math> T: t \mapsto -t.</math>
If the [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian operator]] commutes with the time-reversal operator, that is 
:<math>[H,T]=0,</math>
then, for every energy eigenstate <math>|n\rangle</math>, the time reversed state <math>T|n\rangle</math> is also an eigenstate with the same energy. These two states are sometimes called a '''Kramers pair'''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Fan |last2=Kane |first2=C. L. |last3=Mele |first3=E. J. |date=2013-08-02 |title=Time-Reversal-Invariant Topological Superconductivity and Majorana Kramers Pairs |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.111.056402 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=111 |issue=5 |article-number=056402 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.111.056402|pmid=23952423 |arxiv=1212.4232 |bibcode=2013PhRvL.111e6402Z |s2cid=31559089 }}</ref> In general, this time-reversed state may be identical to the original one, but that is not possible in a half-integer spin system: since time reversal reverses all angular momenta, reversing a half-integer spin cannot yield the same state (the [[magnetic quantum number]] is never zero).

== Mathematical statement and proof ==
In quantum mechanics, the time reversal operation is represented by an [[Antiunitary operator|antiunitary]] operator <math display="inline">T : \mathcal{H} \to \mathcal{H}</math> acting on a [[Hilbert space]] <math display="inline">\mathcal{H}</math>. If it happens that <math display="inline">T^2 = -1</math>, then we have the following simple theorem:

If <math display="inline">T : \mathcal{H} \to \mathcal{H}</math> is an antiunitary operator acting on a Hilbert space <math display="inline">\mathcal{H}</math> satisfying <math display="inline">T^2 = -1</math> and <math display="inline">v</math> a vector in <math display="inline">\mathcal{H}</math>, then <math display="inline">T v</math> is orthogonal to <math display="inline">v</math>.

=== Proof ===
By the definition of an antiunitary operator, <math display="inline">\langle T u, T w \rangle = \langle w, u \rangle</math>, where <math display="inline">u</math> and <math display="inline">w</math> are vectors in <math display="inline">\mathcal{H}</math>. Replacing <math display="inline">u = T v</math> and <math display="inline">w = v</math> and using that <math display="inline">T^2 = -1</math>, we get <math display="inline">\langle T^2 v, T v \rangle = - \langle v, T v \rangle = \langle v, T v \rangle</math>, which implies that <math display="inline">\langle v, T v \rangle = 0</math>.

Consequently, if a [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] <math display="inline">H</math> is time-reversal symmetric, i.e., it commutes with <math display="inline">T,</math> then all its energy [[eigenspace]]s have even degeneracy, since applying <math display="inline">T</math> to an arbitrary energy eigenstate <math display="inline">|n\rangle</math> gives another energy eigenstate <math display="inline">T | n \rangle</math> that is orthogonal to the first one. The orthogonality property is crucial, as it means that the two eigenstates <math display="inline">| n \rangle</math> and <math display="inline">T | n \rangle</math> represent different physical states. If, on the contrary, they were the same physical state, then <math>T |n\rangle = e^{i \alpha} |n\rangle</math> for an angle <math>\alpha \in \mathbb{R}</math>, which would imply

: <math>T^2 |n\rangle = T (e^{i \alpha} |n\rangle) = e^{- i \alpha} e^{i \alpha} |n \rangle = |n \rangle</math>

To complete Kramers degeneracy theorem, we just need to prove that the time-reversal operator <math display="inline">T</math> acting on a [[half-integer|half-odd-integer]] spin Hilbert space satisfies <math display="inline">T^2 = -1</math>. This follows from the fact that the [[spin operator]] <math display="inline">\mathbf{S}</math> represents a type of [[angular momentum]], and, as such, should reverse direction under <math>T</math>:

:<math>\mathbf{S} \to T^{-1} \mathbf{S} T = - \mathbf{S}.</math>

Concretely, an operator <math display="inline">T</math> that has this property is usually written as

: <math>T = e^{- i \pi S_y} K</math>

where <math display="inline">S_y</math> is the spin operator in the <math display="inline">y</math> direction and <math display="inline">K</math> is the complex conjugation map in the <math display="inline">S_z</math> spin basis.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tasaki |first=Hal |title=Physics and mathematics of quantum many-body systems |date=2020 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-030-41265-4 |location=Cham |chapter=2.3: Time-Reversal and Kramers Degeneracy |oclc=1154567924}}</ref>

Since <math display="inline">i S_y</math> has real matrix components in the <math>S_z</math> basis, then

: <math>T^2 = e^{- i \pi S_y} K e^{- i \pi S_y} K = e^{- i 2 \pi S_y} K^2 = (-1)^{2 S}.</math>

Hence, for half-odd-integer spins <math display="inline">S = \frac{1}{2}, \frac{3}{2}, \ldots</math>, we have <math display="inline">T^2 = -1</math>. This is the same minus sign that appears when one does a full <math>2 \pi</math> rotation on [[Spin–statistics theorem|systems with half-odd-integer spins]], such as [[fermion]]s.

== Consequences ==
{{Expand section|date=August 2022}}
The [[energy level]]s of a system with an odd total number of fermions (such as [[electron]]s, [[proton]]s and [[neutron]]s) remain at least doubly [[degenerate energy level|degenerate]] in the presence of purely [[electric field]]s (i.e. no external [[magnetic field]]s). It was first discovered in 1930 by [[Hendrik Anthony Kramers|H. A. Kramers]]<ref>{{cite journal|last=Kramers|first=H. A.|author-link=Hans Kramers|journal= Proceedings of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences|volume=33|issue=6–10|pages=959–972 |year=1930|title=Théorie générale de la rotation paramagnétique dans les cristaux|url=https://www.dwc.knaw.nl/DL/publications/PU00014621.pdf|language=fr}}</ref> as a consequence of the [[Breit equation]]. As shown by [[Eugene Wigner]] in 1932.<ref>E. Wigner, Über die Operation der Zeitumkehr in der Quantenmechanik, Nachr. Akad. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 31, 546–559 (1932) http://www.digizeitschriften.de/dms/img/?PPN=GDZPPN002509032</ref> It is a consequence of the [[time reversal invariance]] of [[electric field]]s, and follows from an application of the [[antiunitary]] ''T''-operator to the wavefunction of an odd number of fermions. The theorem is valid for any configuration of static or time-varying electric fields.

For example, the [[hydrogen]] (H) atom contains one proton and one electron, so that the Kramers theorem does not apply. Indeed, the lowest (hyperfine) energy level of H is nondegenerate, although a generic system might have degeneracy for other reasons. The [[deuterium]] (D) isotope on the other hand contains an extra neutron, so that the total number of fermions is three, and the theorem does apply. The ground state of D contains two hyperfine components, which are twofold and fourfold degenerate.
